newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba rejects some aid from Cuban Americans.
newsitem.headline: Cuba rejects some aid from Cuban Americans.

text.p: Cuba said on Saturday it would reject part of a planeload of food aid for victims of Hurricane Lili sent by Cuban Americans because packages had been adorned with political, "counter-revolutionary" slogans.

The government said in a statement published in the ruling Communist Party newspaper Granma that it had decided to accept "all the cargo that does not have political inscriptions and suggestive, provocative and counter-revolutionary mesages." This amounted to about three quarters of the aid.

But it said the rest of the cargo would be given back to Caritas, the church charity chaneling the aid. The cargo was donated by mostly Cuban-American citizens in the United States and sent through the U.S. church charity Catholic Relief Services and the Roman Catholic diocese in Miami.
It was not clear whether the rejected aid would have to be sent back to the United States.

The aid, consisting of about 30 tonnes of rice, milk and beans, arrived in Havana on a charter flight from Miami a week ago, but had not yet been distributed to areas hit by last month's devastating hurricane.
Officials from Caritas Cuba were not immediately available to comment on the decision announced on Saturday.

Granma said 23 tonnes of rice, beans and canned milk would now be distributed and the remaining seven tonnes handed back. It added that Cuba would never accept "an assault on its dignity", however adverse its circumstances.
It condemned what it called political manipulation in Miami of a "noble and humanitarian" proposal to send aid.

Father Thomas Wenski, an official of the Miami diocese who accompanied the cargo to Cuba, said earlier this week that delays in distributing food appeared due partly to slogans on the cargo and also because the milk component of the cargo came in many varieties. These varieties, including canned and powdered milk, had to be classified by authorities.
Cuban authorities had made clear before the aid was sent that they would not accept political slogans on packages.
According to Wenski, some packages were adorned with mesages such as "exile" and "love can do everything".

"Exile" is a word Cuban authorities do not use about the more than one million Cubans living abroad because it is seen as having a political connotation. "Love can do all" was the title of a pastoral message issued by Cuba's Catholic bishops three years ago that called for political reform in Cuba.
Authorities have said Hurricane Lili, which swept central and western areas of Cuba on Oct. 17-18, destroyed 5,000 homes and damaged crops, power lines and communications.

The Cuban American community in Florida mobilized rapidly to send aid, although some hardline critics of President Fidel Castro argued against sending anything, saying assistance would just serve to prop up the government.
The U.S. government 10 days ago waived a ban on direct flights to the communist-ruled island in order to allow the relief flight to take place.
